analysis.one_liner: Raises federal fuel economy standards for new cars and light trucks by 20-40 percent over their 1988 levels.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill, but floor action died when a debate-ending vote got 57 of the 60 votes it needed on September 25, 1990, and the Senate never took an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required each automaker to raise the average fuel economy of its new passenger cars by 20 percent over its 1988 level for model years 1995 through 2000, and by 40 percent for 2001 and beyond, with caps of 40 and 45 miles per gallon. It would have imposed the first legislatively set standards for light trucks, set up a process to adjust the post-2001 standards, required annual EPA testing of real-world fuel economy, and doubled fines for repeat violators. The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee in June 1990 but never got an up-or-down vote in the full Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save money at the pump as new cars and light trucks became significantly more efficient; the bill's own findings cite roughly $30 billion in driver savings from earlier efficiency gains, and estimate that stopping the 1989 rollback alone would have saved 900 million gallons of fuel over the vehicles' lives. It would also benefit the country at large through reduced dependence on imported oil and lower carbon dioxide emissions, which the bill says contribute to global warming.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and taxpayers through lower fuel use

how_it_helps.text: Sets each manufacturer's car standard at its own 1988 average plus 20 percent for model years 1995-2000 and plus 40 percent for 2001 and after, capped at 40 and 45 miles per gallon, so each automaker must improve rather than coast at the old 27.5 mpg floor.

Extends fuel economy requirements to light trucks, which the bill notes had grown to about one-third of new passenger vehicle sales with little fuel-economy improvement since 1982, setting floors of 20 mpg and caps of 30 mpg (1995-2000) and 35 mpg (2001 and after).
Doubles the civil penalty for manufacturers that violate the standard in three consecutive years, giving the standard teeth.
Requires annual EPA reports comparing official test results with real-world driving, addressing the gap between sticker mileage and actual performance that drivers experience.

Directs the National Academy of Sciences to assess remaining fuel-efficiency potential and recommend research priorities, and the Energy Department to study options for regulating efficiency beyond 2001.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would have borne the engineering and compliance costs of raising fleet mileage, costs that would have been partly passed to buyers as higher new-vehicle prices; and oil companies and gasoline sellers, which would have sold less fuel over time. Some buyers could have faced tradeoffs in vehicle size or performance as manufacturers retooled.

drawbacks.text: Stricter standards would have raised the engineering and production costs of new vehicles, some portion of which typically shows up as higher sticker prices for buyers, even though the bill requires the Transportation Secretary to weigh consumer costs against lifetime fuel savings in any post-2001 adjustment.

Mileage mandates can push manufacturers toward smaller or lighter vehicles, a tradeoff critics raised at the time, though the bill allows standards to be adjusted for post-2001 years if the maximum feasible level is lower than the formula requires.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and durable: less fuel bought every year, lower oil imports, and lower emissions, with the bill's own findings documenting that past efficiency standards paid for themselves many times over in driver savings. The costs are real but front-loaded — higher vehicle prices during a transition to more efficient fleets — and the bill's per-manufacturer baseline design and adjustment process moderate the burden. On balance the benefits outweighed the costs, which is why the bill's failure left consumers paying more at the pump than they otherwise would have.

outcome.mechanism: After the Commerce Committee approved it, the bill died when the Senate failed by three votes to cut off debate on the committee's version, sent it back to the calendar, and never held an up-or-down vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Bryan introduced the bill on June 22, 1989, joined by Senators Hollings, Gorton, and Lieberman, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The bill had 26 Senate cosponsors, 21 Democrats and 5 Republicans.
The Senate Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on April 3, 1990, and reported it on June 11 with a written report, though minority views were filed.
On September 14, 1990, the Senate voted 68-28 to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed, clearing the way for debate; 45 Democrats and 23 Republicans voted yes.

On September 25, 1990, a cloture vote on the committee substitute — a vote needing 60 senators to end debate and allow a final vote — failed 57-42, with 42 Democrats and 15 Republicans in favor and 29 Republicans and 13 Democrats opposed, and the bill was returned to the calendar.
No further action occurred before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill never received an up-or-down vote in the Senate and never reached the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The automakers and oil sellers who would have borne the cost of the standards were better off, since no higher mileage requirements were enacted in that Congress. Buyers who value larger or more powerful vehicles also kept that choice, at the cost of continued high fuel consumption by the fleet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers that avoided higher mileage mandates

sides.party_line_note: Both cloture votes showed a Democratic majority against a mostly Republican opposition: 45-9 among Democrats and 23-19 among Republicans on the motion to proceed, then 42-13 among Democrats and 15-29 among Republicans on the failed debate-ending vote, where opposition was concentrated in the Republican caucus.

industries.note: The bill would have required each maker to lift its new-car and light-truck fleet mileage 20-40 percent above 1988 levels, imposing major engineering and compliance costs and letting regulators double fines on repeat violators. Its gain from the bill's failure was continued sales of less efficient vehicles, a cost that shows up as higher fuel bills for drivers.

Higher mileage standards directly reduce gasoline demand, and the bill's findings count past efficiency gains in barrels of oil per day saved. Lower fuel sales mean lower revenue for oil producers and refiners.

industries.industry: Used-car buyers and households that cannot buy new
industries.note: Higher new-car prices tend to push demand into the used market, raising used-car prices, while fuel savings from fleet turnover take years to reach households that keep vehicles a long time. The bill offered no direct relief to non-buyers.
